reviews.review: Loud angry giant men screaming at each other. 10/10

Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine is a 3rd person shooter.
I've played all Warhammer 40,000 video games. Some were good, and others were so great that I still play them, even several years after their release.


This is one of the best 40k games, period. It nails everything- from what makes a good 3rd person shooter, to what makes a true-to-lore 40k game. 

To start off, This isn't your standard 3rd person-totally-not-gears-of-war game. Whilst most 3PSs focus on a cover system, Space Marine removes that entirely. You ARE the cover. You can wade into a mob of enemies, without dying every 3 seconds. It perfectly encapsulates what makes a space marine a space marine, and lets you experience that firsthand.

The combat is divided into two parts- ranged and melee. You are given a wide variety of weapons to slaughter your enemies in different and uniquely brutal ways. Each weapon feels (and sounds!) exactly how it should. The shot of a bolter, the hiss of a meltagun, and the roar of a plasma cannon. And although the ranged weapons are cool, the melee weapons are even better. Chainswords (chainsaw-swords) evicerate and rend flesh whenever they strike, turning a large horde of orks into a bloody mess very quickly. Thunder hammers, although slow, deal tremendous damage and completly pulverise your enemies. The combat (especially in single player or the horde-mode) is immensly satisfying and one of the best parts of the game.

The game has both a single-player and a multiplayer. The single player has a decently lengthy campaign (10-12 hours) with a pretty good story. It does have its faults (unfinished story arcs that will probably never get finished b/c r.i.p THQ). The multiplayer, although good and reasonably well balanced, gets repedative with the 4 maps (excluding expansions). You also can't choose which side you are on pre-match, meaning you might not even get to see your shiny new color scheme for a couple matches. The multiplayer also follows the standard 'level up to improve' philosophy, with special perks unlocked by completing challenges (some of which are brutally difficult without help). 

Overall, this is a fantastic 40k game that really makes you feel like you are playing a space marine.
It's practically a badass simulator, 10/10 from me.

*Single Player* Review only, 

The game has two modes.
Non interactive cutscenes, or "semi interactive" cutscenes. 

1) The "story" of this game is fully in service of the "Warhammer 40k" license. Mechncally the story isn't trying to do anything you haven't seen a million times in *all* other types of media. 

However, the story is very good at providing you with the "feel" of the Warhammer 40k setting. If you are not interested in this license, don't get this game for it's narrative experience.

The graphics engine, some of the art assets, and physics engine all feel like they were in a lot of other games in the ps3/xbox1 generation. 

The sound and music are not trying to make an artistic statement of note. 

2)

This game is a third-person restricted shooters (only carry 3 guns at once, and one of these guns is never going to be used). 

This game is also a third-person melee combat. 

The amount of verbs you can use seems extremely empowering for the first 1/3-1/2 of the game. 
But
The third person shooting becomes tedious because you have so few guns available. 
The melee combat becomes tedious because you only really get 2 combos to use. The melee combat also has "execution" cutscenes, but only has about 6 -8 of them total. You may execute well over 100 enemies in a playthrough. 

Ideally the game wants you to interchangbly use ranged and melee so as to not over rely on any one system. 

However

The fatal flaw of the "gameplay" of this game is that toward the halfway point of the game, the game starts to give you many enemies with very powerful ranged weapons.  
This creates a "trial and error" type of gameplay loop. Because if you're about to get into a situation where there are several of these types of enemies, you will probably die because you don't realize where they are all located before you can shoot them. 

However, once you know where these enemies will stay, then it becomes quite easy to just target them at the start of an encounter. 

Ranged enemies with heavy firepower  is the main way that the game creates challenge from 1/3-3/3 of the game. 

If the game had made the melee combat system more robust, then they could create challenge through melee combat, while allowing the shooting to just be a secondary system. 

But you will mostly win or lose in the late game based on your ability to quickly shoot things which do 90 percent of the damage toward you otherwise. 


3) 

I still recommend this game, it tries to be an experience. And it feels a lot less cynical than many other big-budget games of that console generation.
